articles.title_orig: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.title_zh: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.content_orig:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.
With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience .
The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.
According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.
For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World : “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”
An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology , cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.
“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”
Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”
To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.
Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.
Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.
There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”
Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.
For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags , most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.
Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”
But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii ] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”
While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

articles.title_zh: U.S. and China agree to "super intelligence" dialogue amid AI tensions
articles.content_orig:
High-stakes discussions on trade and artificial intelligence unfold in New York City as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer meet with Chinese officials. Fox News contributor Dan Hoffman analyzes this strategic framework between the world's two most powerful nations ahead of the upcoming summit with President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The United States and China agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion in goods traded between the two countries after a three-day summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C.
According to the White House, the $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions apply to "non-sensitive goods."
U.S. exports, including agricultural products, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices will receive favorable tariff treatment in China. Meanwhile, U.S. imports of Chinese-made small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children's car seats will also receive preferential treatment.
The agreement was reached through the U.S.-China Board of Trade, a body first proposed during Trump's visit to China in May and formally established during Xi's visit to Washington this week.
President Donald Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to speak during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House Sept. 24, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE'
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC Friday that "a lot more details" about the new trade agreement will be released Monday.
Greer said the tariff terms were hammered out after weeks of negotiations. Neither country has released the final tariff rates or all the products that will receive favored status going forward.
This marks one of the most significant cooldowns in the trade war Trump launched against China in February 2025, when he levied a 10% tariff on all Chinese imports, citing Beijing's alleged role in the fentanyl crisis and illegal immigration. China hit back with levies on U.S. coal, liquefied natural gas, crude oil and cars.
President Donald Trump holds up a tariff chart while speaking during a "Make America Wealthy Again" trade announcement event in the Rose Garden at the White House April 2, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
BESSENT REVEALS EXTENSION TO BUSAN AGREEMENT WITH CHINA UNTIL JANUARY
At their peak, U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods reached a staggering 145% in April 2025, shortly after Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" reciprocal tariffs. China responded with tariffs of up to 125% on U.S. goods.
U.S. and Chinese negotiators met in Geneva in May 2025 and agreed to a 90-day truce that lowered U.S. tariffs to 30% and China's to 10%. The agreement was extended for another 90 days in August.
President Donald Trump walks on a red carpet after greeting Chinese President Xi Jinping during an arrival ceremony Sept. 23, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Trump and Xi reached another tentative agreement during talks in South Korea in October 2025. Under the deal, China agreed to crack down on fentanyl precursors, resume purchases of U.S. soybeans and ease restrictions on rare-earth exports , while the United States agreed to further ease tariffs.
The two countries will now use the Board of Trade to negotiate additional tariff reductions and other trade disputes, leaving open the possibility of broader agreements in the months ahead.

articles.title_orig: Iced Coffee At A Job Interview? Career Experts Weigh In On Viral Debate
articles.title_zh: Iced Coffee At A Job Interview? Career Experts Weigh In On Viral Debate
articles.content_orig:
Would you reject a job candidate who brought an iced coffee to an interview? Your answer may not matter: Either way, someone on the internet thinks you're wrong. And a career expert says she's over it.
The iced coffee debate, currently taking place on social media platforms across the web, reflects "everything wrong with hiring right now," says Phoebe Gavin, a Washington, D.C.-based career and leadership coach.
The conversation started with a corporate recruiter's Sept. 16 TikTok video post about Gen Z candidates bringing iced coffees to job interviews. Her take: Drinking an iced coffee in an interview "looks a little too casual" and could hurt your chances of landing the role.
The video, which has over 465,000 views on TikTok as of Friday afternoon, sparked a fierce discussion that quickly spread to other platforms. Some commenters on the original video argued that bringing an iced coffee has no bearing on a candidate's qualifications: "What does that have to do with their work ethic, experience, or intelligence?"
Others agreed with the recruiter: "It's not about coffee, it's about professionalism."
The conversation is reflective of a broken job market because it shows how "the power dynamic is so, so, so skewed toward the employer," Gavin says.
In her view, it's "wildly unfair" for hirers to prioritize something as trivial as a beverage over a candidate's qualifications. "You've spent hours and hours and hours on these [job] applications," she says. "You have 10 years of work experience and a master's degree. And a coffee is the reason why you don't get that job?"
In one sense, the iced coffee debate is really about the "injustice of the hiring process," says Gavin.
Many job seekers feel desperate and exhausted after months of searching : Over a quarter of unemployed workers, 27%, have been looking for a role for over half a year, according to August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
For someone struggling to land a job right now, "the idea of being rejected because you were thirsty is just enraging," Gavin says.
In another sense, the iced coffee debate represents a "battle of the generations" between Gen Z and older workers, says Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications and career expert at LinkedIn.
"Gen Z has brought in a different perspective on work," Fisher says: They bring "a little bit more of their personality" to the office, and they're more likely to "challenge some of these corporate norms ."
Despite the online furor, there's no hard evidence that Gen Zers are more or less likely to bring an iced coffee to an interview than anyone else. They may simply be more likely to push back against workplace rules or standards that seem arbitrary or outdated to them, says Fisher.
But what Gen Z sees as reasonable pushback can seem unprofessional to older workers, says Jamie Close, a corporate recruiter at staffing and recruiting company HireQuest.
For some hirers, Close says, seeing a young candidate bring an iced coffee to an interview reinforces some workplace stereotypes: "They're going to have that Gen Z mentality. They're going to be lazy. They're not going to fit in."
From Close's perspective, whether a candidate brings in a beverage is "not what sticks with me as a recruiter at the end of the day."
"If they're a great candidate, I don't care if they brought an iced coffee," she says.
But since other hirers may have different opinions, you might as well leave your iced coffee in the car, says Close. "You don't want any distractions. You don't want to spill. You don't want to have all that noise," she says. "We just want to focus on you and your interest in the job."
Fisher agrees: It's "kind of ridiculous" that an iced coffee could be a deciding factor in whether a candidate gets an offer, but "in such a competitive job market, you actually do need to think about these things."
Setting yourself up for success means keeping the focus on your skills and experience, and avoiding anything that could detract from your interview performance, she says. You wouldn't want to show up late or mispronounce your interviewer's name, for example.
In short: "Just don't risk it," says Fisher.
In Gavin's view, rejecting an applicant for bringing an iced coffee says more about the interviewer — and the workplace environment they represent — than it does about the candidate. For one, it could indicate that they're uptight or overly focused on appearances, she says.
If you're able to be choosy about your next opportunity, take it as a sign that their company wasn't a good fit for you, Gavin says. "Be glad that they pulled you out of the process for showing up with a beverage."
If you're in a position where you have to consider every opportunity — which many job seekers are, Gavin says — make sure to ask plenty of questions about the workplace culture. "You may or may not be able to use that information to say 'no' to a position, but at the very least, you'd be able to go in with eyes wide open," she says.
Keep in mind that a job interview goes both ways, Fisher notes: You're evaluating the company just as much as they're evaluating you. Job seekers should walk into each interview with a clear idea of what kind of work environment they're looking for, she says, whether that's a buttoned-up, traditional office with a formal dress code or a laid-back one that welcomes hoodies and jeans. Maybe you're trying to strike a good balance between those two ends of the spectrum.
But "if you feel like you really have to like play a certain role, and that doesn't feel comfortable for you, it might not be the right place for you," says Fisher.
As for the interviewers, they should give job seekers "a bit of grace," she adds. "They're probably really nervous. They've been going through it. It's a hard job market out there, so try to look beyond those kind of superficial things and really focus on, 'Is this person going to be successful in this role?'"

articles.title_orig: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.title_zh: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG — Ronald Sakolsky never thought his money would go this far.
What was once a vast, dry desert in northern China has transformed into a lush, green forest of 50,000 full-grown trees, thanks in part to a $5,000 donation he made more than a quarter century ago to a local farmer and “sand-control worker” named Yin Yuzhen.
Sakolsky, 69, a retired teacher from Pennsylvania, was amazed to see the transformation in China’s Inner Mongolia region last month when he visited for the first time in 26 years.
“Seeing it with my own eyes, that was the biggest surprise,” he told Chinese state media. “I saw pictures, I was told all about it, but until you see it is when you realize that it’s real.”
Sakolsky and Yin’s reunion last month has been held up by Chinese authorities as an example of how China and the United States, the world’s two biggest greenhouse gas emitters, can work together on global issues such as climate change .
Chinese leader Xi Jinping , in Washington this week for a summit with President Donald Trump , mentioned Sakolsky’s story in his toast at a state dinner on Thursday, saying it “touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between our two peoples.”
Sakolsky was teaching English on exchange in China’s central Henan province in 1999 when he saw a TV news report about Yin. More than a decade earlier, the newly married Yin had started planting trees as a way to feel less isolated in her new home in the Mu Us Desert, also known as the Maowusu Desert (“bad water” in Mongolian).
Moved by her story, Sakolsky raised $5,000, which was many times Yin’s annual income, so she could plant even more. They met in person in 2000, when Yin promised Sakolsky that she and her family would take good care of the saplings.
Earlier this year, Yin launched an online campaign to track down Sakolsky, and last month he made a 10-day visit to China that included an emotional reunion with Yin in her forest, where the trees now stand more than 30 feet high and the government has named a grove after him.
The two of them planted a friendship tree, and Sakolsky collected a jar of sand to take home to Pennsylvania. Yin also gave him a cross-stitch with the words “One Earth, One Dream.”
“I want him to know that I kept my word, and that Chinese people keep our promises,” she said. Yin called Sakolsky her “brother” and said the sapling they planted together would be standing tall in another 26 years.
Reports on Sakolsky’s visit have been heavily promoted by Chinese authorities and widely viewed on Chinese social media, where commenters described him as “a real friend of Chinese people.”
Tree-planting efforts are part of a decadeslong government campaign sometimes referred to as China’s “Great Green Wall,” which was launched in 1978 as a 73-year effort intended to reduce sandstorms and help stave off desertification associated with global climate change.
Away from emotional stories like Yin’s, the campaign has had mixed success. While the Great Green Wall is a “great initiative in principle,” the Chinese government tends to emphasize “top-down, technocratic solutions to environmental problems” and focus on targets more than quality, said Judith Shapiro, who teaches at American University in the department of environment, development and health. The loss of open land for nomadic herding as a result of the initiative “remains a serious blow to some ethnic minority nationalities,” she said.
In the program’s early years, deserts were lined with “fast-growing but water-hungry” trees such as poplars that depleted water tables, though more suitable and biodiverse species are now being planted. “Overall, the Chinese government has done a good job instilling the idea that trees are a great benefit to society,” Shapiro said.
Days after Sakolsky met with Yin in China’s arid north, a likely impact of the changing climate was felt when a devastating flood struck 2,000 miles away along the Nepal-China border. More than 1,400 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after the Aug. 26 disaster, which experts say was linked to warming temperatures in the Himalayas.
“I am very, very sad for the people in Nepal and people in China,” Sakolsky said at a news conference in Beijing on Aug. 31. “I know now the world is alive, and if I keep throwing paper on the ground or if I keep letting trees die, I am killing the life of the world, which means I am actually killing mankind.”
The Tibet flood was one of several disasters this summer in China, where flooding triggered by Tropical Storm Maysak in early July killed at least 159 people in the southern region of Guangxi. At least 16 people in Jiangxi province were killed in a Sept. 5 mudslide set off by torrential rain linked to Typhoon Saudel. Researchers said last year that climate change is making such storms in Asia more frequent and severe.
China says it plans to reach peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. Its carbon emissions have been “flat or falling” since 2024 and are on track to fall in 2026 for the second year in a row, according to an analysis for Carbon Brief this month by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
While its coal emissions are still rising, China is seeking to fill a void in global climate leadership left by the U.S., the world’s largest carbon emitter historically, which withdrew from the Paris climate agreement during Trump’s first days back in office last year. Critics say China’s goals are too cautious and will leave it unable to meet its Paris Agreement pledge to cut emissions by 65% from 2005 to 2030.
Trump and Xi were not expected to have any meaningful discussion about climate change at their summit this week.
Sakolsky said last month that both countries have common interests, including combating climate change.
“You want the best for your children because you know they are tomorrow,” he said. “You want the best for your country, but it does not mean you have to sacrifice your children.”
Sakolsky called on anyone inspired by his friendship with Yin to “go out and plant one tree.”
“If everybody plants one tree in their backyard or in their park after watching this,” he said, “can you imagine how many trees we would have in the world?”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Erin Tan and Fred Dufour from Beijing.
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.
Erin Tan is a news researcher in NBC News’s Beijing bureau.
Fred Dufour is an NBC cameraman based in China.

articles.title_orig: China’s newest panda diplomats Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are en route to Atlanta
articles.title_zh: China’s newest panda diplomats Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are en route to Atlanta
articles.content_orig:
Two giant pandas have left China on a flight bound for their new home at a zoo in Atlanta, the latest emissaries in Beijing’s long tradition of using “panda diplomacy” to strengthen ties with other countries.
They departed Chengdu, in southwestern China, at 2:55 a.m. Sunday morning local time (2:55 p.m. ET Saturday), China’s state news agency Xinhua said. The flight came just a day after Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington concluded.
During that visit, which was intended to address rising US-China tensions, Xi and US President Donald Trump extended a trade truce and agreed to establish an AI hotline between the two countries.
Video from Xinhua showed fans waving placards as trucks carrying the pandas headed to the airport, from the Giant Panda Breeding Research Base in Sichuan province. Vehicles then towed two crates to the plane before they were lifted into it ahead of their journey, expected to last about 15 hours.
China also arranged for several veterinarians and breeders to remain at the zoo in Atlanta as the pandas enter quarantine upon arrival, the agency added.
The team at Zoo Atlanta and the Chinese team held “many online and offline meetings to carry out in-depth exchanges on the upgrading and transformation plan” for the venue that houses the pandas, which will be on loan from the Chinese government, according to Xinhua.
“What Zoo Atlanta has been working hard for the past year is making improvements to our enclosures, where our enclosures are a lot bigger,” Sam Rivera, the zoo’s vice president of animal health, told Xinhua. “We’re ensuring that we have plenty of bamboo for them to eat. We have experienced keepers that are trained on taking care of giant pandas.”
Rare, fluffy and irresistibly cute, pandas are adored across the globe. The animals once roamed a vast swath of China, along with parts of northern Myanmar and Vietnam, but human encroachment and climate change shrank the habitat of the bamboo-munching bears to just six mountain ranges above the Sichuan basin, deep in China’s hinterland.
Hailed in imperial times as the “land of heavenly abundance,” Sichuan is now better known as the “hometown of pandas.” The mountainous province boasts a latticework of panda nature reserves and breeding centers, all built in recent decades as China – and the world – raced to save the multimillion-years-old “living fossil” from extinction.
Provincial capital Chengdu – a sprawling metropolis known for its spicy hotpot and old tea houses – sits at the foot of snow-capped mountains with misty old-growth forests where wild pandas still roam.
The city’s panda breeding base is the largest in the country, housing more than 240 bears – or a third of the world’s captive panda population. The sprawling facility draws up to 11 million visitors a year, on par with Shanghai Disneyland.
Loaning pandas has long been a tool of Chinese diplomacy, following a decades-long government effort to transform them from a little-known animal into a cultural icon and national symbol. For more than half a century, Beijing has dispatched these charismatic animals overseas to shore up alliances, mend estranged ties and court new partners.
“The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans,” Xi said on Thursday , referencing the half-century in which pandas lived in US zoos on loan from the Chinese government. That tradition was started by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1972, shortly after Richard Nixon became the first US president to visit China following the Communist Party’s rise to power in 1949.
One of the pandas bound for Atlanta even has the same name – Ping Ping, meaning “peace” – as the first ever panda Mao gifted to the Soviet Union in 1957. He was born on March 17, 2020, has large black patches around his eyes and is especially good at climbing trees, according to China’s National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
China is more in love with its pandas than ever. That’s complicated matters for Beijing
The other panda, Fu Shuang, meaning “double blessings,” was born seven months later on October 18. She has a small tuft of fur on the top of her head, a slightly protruding forehead and finds food very easily, the administration said.
In a report ahead of their upcoming journey, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV asked their keeper to describe the pair.
Ping Ping “is brave and gentle,” Fu Jia said. “During training sessions, when he spots me holding an apple, he will make soft whimpering sounds, eager for the treat.”
Fu Shuang, on the other hand, “is crazy about honey,” she said.
Zookeepers at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding selected the pair after considering their age, health, genetics and personality.
“They should be docile and like each other, and hopefully be able to mate naturally,” the park’s deputy director Li Mingxi told Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
They are scheduled to arrive in Atlanta early on Sunday morning local time. The zoo has hosted several pandas before. Another pair, Lun Lun and Yang Yang, had seven offspring there between 2006 and 2016 before returning to Chengdu.
Zoo Atlanta earlier in the year said it would be “delighted and honored” to welcome the two pandas.
A banner displayed at the zoo on Saturday read “The future home of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang.”
A Zoo Atlanta representative said the facility would not share information about Ping Ping and Fu Shuang’s planned arrival date, and declined to comment further.
Chinese officials and the Atlanta zoo “will carry out in-depth academic and cultural exchanges to continuously enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the people of China and the United States,” Xinhua said.
Panda diplomacy has offered some relief from the tensions increasingly shaping the US-China relationship in recent years, as the two countries compete in an AI arms race and engage in a spiraling trade war.
Two giant pandas arrived in San Diego in June 2024, the first time China allowed new pandas to travel to the US in more than two decades. A second pair traveled to Washington’s National Zoo later that year.
In preparation for the move, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang have been quarantined for a month with a roster of live-in carers, Li said. The pandas have been trained for their long flight too, becoming used to their crate and loud noises.
Late Saturday night, China’s ambassador to the US Xie Feng shared photos of the two pandas on his X account and said they were on their way.
“Get ready to greet our two fluffy stars!” he wrote.
Their departure would be a sad one for, Fu, their keeper.
“After caring for them for so long… It’s like raising your own children,” she told CCTV.
“They weighed barely over 100 grams at birth, and we nurtured them until they grew big and heavy. I won’t get to see them for quite a long time, so it’s hard to say goodbye.”
CNN’s Xiaoqian Lin, Farida Elsebai, Rebekah Riess, Eduardo Cuevas and Mitchell McCluskey contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: The other crop that built China: how millet became foundation for Chinese civilisation
articles.content_orig:
While domestication of rice was crucial in southern China, it was millet that ruled the North, laying groundwork for birth of the country
Rice may be the most universal ingredient in the world, serving as a cornerstone of the diet for billions in Asia.
However, for much of Chinese history, rice faced a serious competitor, and entire cultures developed around a different cereal grain, one that has since diminished in significance: millet.
Millet is a cereal grain that behaves and tastes similarly to rice but has a rounder form. It is often used in porridge, stir-fries, or even fritters. In certain regions of China, millet is favoured as a food for pregnant women, with millet porridge being particularly gentle on the stomach. Despite this, it cannot rival the cultural importance of rice.
Yet, the domestication of millet, along with other cereals globally, stands as one of the most pivotal events in human history. Its domestication fundamentally altered natural landscapes and enabled humans to control the plants they consume, as opposed to surviving at the mercy of wild crops.

articles.title_zh: At least 27 people killed in 2 mass shootings in South Africa's Johannesburg, Capetown
articles.content_orig:
At least 27 people were killed in two mass shootings in South Africa's two main cities, police said on Sunday.
The first incident occurred Saturday evening when eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed a bar west of Johannesburg and shot 17 people and wounded 15 others.
The suspects opened fire on customers drinking outside and then moved inside to continue shooting, police said, where they killed 13 males and four females.
The motive for the shooting was still unknown, police said, adding that the suspects torched two vehicles before fleeing.
In a separate shooting at an entertainment venue in a township outside Cape Town early on Sunday, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more.
Five of the victims were declared dead at the scene while the others succumbed to their injuries while being taken to hospital.
No suspect has been arrested in either case, police said.
The attacks come as South Africa, awash with legal and illegal firearms, grapples with persistent gun violence often linked to gang rivalries and competition among informal businesses.
The country of about 62 million people records roughly 60 murders a day, among the highest rates globally.
In March, soldiers moved into violence hotspots in Johannesburg to support police efforts to tackle rampant crime, described by President Cyril Ramaphosa as one of the biggest threats facing the country.
South Africa has repeatedly turned to the army in times of crisis, from enforcing strict Covid-19 lockdowns in 2020 to deploying troops during the deadly riots sparked by the jailing of ex-president Jacob Zuma in 2021.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

China's Song Jiayuan, right, and Zhang Linru hold their flags after competing in the women's shot put final at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Credit: AP/Lee Jin-man
NAGOYA, Japan — They're called the Asian Games. But more aptly, they should be called the “China Games,” another chapter in country’s four-decade domination of the continental, multisports championships.
Midway through the two-week event, China has won 107 gold medals with Japan on 31 in second place. The overall medal total is closer, but China still leads Japan 176 to 129 through Saturday's results.
These Asian Games involve at least 11,000 athletes. That's more than the Summer Olympics two years ago in Paris with about 10,700. And similar to the Olympics, the gap is very wide between the sporting haves, and the have-nots.
At the bottom of the medal table, four countries have only one bronze medal — Bangladesh, Brunei, Mongolia and Syria. And another half dozen countries have yet to win any medals
The six-day swimming competition dominated the first week, and here China piled up 30 golds. Freestyler Zhang Zhanshuo won seven golds and four came in every freestyle distance: the 200-meter, 400, 800 and 1,500. He also added gold in three relays.

Chinese 13-year-old Yu Zidi picked up three golds — 200 butterfly and the 200 and 400 individual medleys. Both swimmers will be forces at the world championships next year in Budapest, Hungary, and the Los Angeles Olympics the year after that.
Despite China's power, the only world record went to Japan's Shin Ohashi, who set the world mark in the 200 breaststroke (2 minutes, 4.83 seconds).
The flags of China and Japan are raised during the medal ceremony for the men's rings final in artistic gymnastics at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: AP/Eugene Hoshiko
It has been rough sailing for organizers and the Olympic Council of Asia. Organizers decided against building a dedicated athletes village, a move to contain spending. Instead, athletes and officials have been lodged on a cruise ship, in hotels, and in temporary wood huts.
Early complaints included beds that are too short, leaky roofs, and mix-ups in room assignment with women booked in with men.
Attendance has also been sparse in some venues, and transportation has been spotty with some venues located far from host city Nagoya.
Organizers have openly apologized.
Gold medalist, China team, pose with their national flag, after the women's 4 x 200-meter freestyle relay final in swimming at the Asian Games in Tokyo, Japan, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: AP/Hiro Komae
“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport,” Satoshi Murate, organizing committee general secretary, told a Saturday news conference. “I frankly apologize for the mistakes.”
Japan won the bid for these games in 2016. That was before the pandemic, before the Tokyo Olympics were delayed until 2021, and before bid scandals linked to the Tokyo Games were uncovered.
Momentum for big spending was lost.
The final price tag for the Tokyo Olympics was $ 13 billion, though a government audit suggested it was twice that much. In the wake, there was limited interests from sponsors and others to match that spending for the Asian Games.
Organizers were also embarrassed during the first week when the North Korean national anthem was played at a men's field hockey match between South Korea and Bangladesh.
Chances are you have never seen many of these sports. There's kabaddi, which looks like a physical game of tag, sepaktakraw (foot volleyball), kurash (wrestling with roots in Uzbekistan), jiu jitsu, padel, soft tennis, teqball and wushu.
Of course, there are all the old Olympic standbys such as track and field, tennis, swimming, badminton, gymnastics, soccer, cycling, weightlifting, and so forth.
Esports are also in the Asian Games for the second time following the games in China three years ago. On Saturday 11-year-old Japanese schoolboy Yuki Kurihara won a gold medal.
Mixed martial arts is also being included for the first time with a long-shot eye at landing in the Olympics.
The version in the Asian Games can be described as “MMA Light,” fighting without the cage. Fighters wear gloves and shin pads, elbow blows are banned, and no knees or kicks to the head are allowed when a fighter is on the ground.

articles.title_zh: College football scores, results: Oregon tops USC, Texas hangs on to beat Tennessee in Week 4 action
articles.content_orig:
After a wild first few weeks of the college football season, we had our best slate yet in Week 4 and it did not disappoint.
The day started with a marquee showdown between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee , and the Longhorns won rights to the 'UT' moniker with a tough defensive performance. Texas' Colin Simmons tied a school record with five sacks in a 20-17 win — though he did get in a bit of trouble after his first .
No. 17 Iowa provided the drama for the day in the afternoon, driving the length of the field in the final minute and scoring on a walk-off TD pass from Hank Brown to Reece Vander Zee as time expired to beat No. 18 Michigan 20-19 . Elsewhere, No. 4 Ole Miss got shelled by No. 21 Florida , No. 2 Georgia throttled Oklahoma in an ugly game for Sooners QB John Mateer and No. 15 Utah held on for a 31-17 win at Iowa State .
In the evening, No. 20 Oregon kept its conference title and playoff hopes alive with a clutch road win at No. 12 USC, but paid a price. QB Dante Moore was knocked out of the game after a scary collision . Dylan Raiola replaced him and led the Ducks to an impressive 41-27 win .
In other action, Lane Kiffin and No. 10 LSU bounced back after their disappointing loss to Ole Miss last week with a beatdown of No. 23 Texas A&M and No. 8 Alabama rolled to a 49-18 win over South Carolina .
Follow all of the action with live updates, highlights and analysis below:
Minnesota QB Drake Lindsey already has 2 TD passes, including this 9-yarder to Jalen Smith.
Minnesota 14, Washington 0 | End 1st
The Tigers weren't able to do anything with their final possession, so the Bulldogs will hold on for the SEC win to remain undefeated.
Kamario Taylor logged another Heisman-worthy performance with 360 passing yards and 3 TDs.
The Tigers' defense did its job. Now the offense has 51 seconds to go from their own 47.
The Bulldogs are likely going to pull off the win after the Tigers couldn't match Kamario Taylor's touchdown drive. Missouri got all the way down to the MSU 11, but consecutive passes fell incomplete before a turnover on downs.
The Tigers do still have 3 timeouts left with just over 1 minute left in the game.
Koi Perich intercepted USC QB Jayden Maiava in the end zone on the Trojans' last-ditch drive. Impressive road win for the Ducks, who played most of the game with a backup QB.
The Bulldogs have retaken the lead on a bullet pass from Kamario Taylor to Sanfrisco Magee.
What a drive for Mississippi State!
The Tigers have bounced back and remain in contention for a playoff spot after their disappointing loss to Ole Miss a week ago.
Sam Leavitt was 17-for-23 passing for 312 yards, 2 TDs and 1 pick. LSU's backup QB Landen Clark scored two rushing TDs. A&M's Marcel Reed struggled all night, as did everybody else in an Aggie uniform.
Kamario Taylor and Mississippi State are getting the ball right back after a quick possession by Missouri. There's just under 6 minutes left in the fourth quarter.
Jordon Davison powers his way into the end zone from 2 yards out, and that should pretty much put this one away for the Ducks with 2:03 to play.
The Bulldogs have tied it back up after a gritty 14-play, 73-yard drive is capped off by a short TD run by Fluff Bothwell. We have a close one in Starkville.
Missouri 24, MSU 24 | 7:09 left
Heisman hopeful Kamario Taylor is hobbled but still doing everything he can to keep the Bulldogs in the game. They're in scoring range and nearing the red zone as the game ticks inside the 10-minute mark.
The Trojans go for a 4th-and-7 from their own 49 but Jayden Maiava's pass is broken up. Oregon has the ball back with a 34-27 lead and 7:15 to play.
Dylan Raiola lofts a moon ball into the waiting arms of Dakorien Moore for a 29-yard TD strike. The Ducks' drive was kept alive by a questionable roughing the QB penalty on USC on a 3rd-and-long.
The Tigers have taken the lead on another TD pass from Austin Simmons to Cayden Lee. This one is for 28 yards and Missouri has scored 24 straight now.
Missouri 24, MSU 17 | 3 minutes left in Q3
Jayden Maiava and the USC offense is dialed in right now. He fires an 11-yard TD pass to Tanook Hines and it's a new ballgame in LA.
USC 27, Oregon 27 | 12:41 to play
The USC defense finally got a stop of the Ducks and it now has the ball with a chance to tie it up, trailing 27-20.
The Tigers are rolling. It's backup QB Landen Clark with his second short touchdown run of the game.
It's getting good in Starkville. The Bulldogs just knotted the game at 17-17 on a field goal with just under 5 minutes left in the third quarter.
The Aggies have doubled their point total on the night after an interception of Sam Leavitt led to a field goal.

articles.content_orig:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”
During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during Knicks’ NBA Finals games.
“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”
The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.
Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL'
“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”
Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.
“Can you foul out of ‘SNL?’” Towns asked.
In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson portrayed a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”
It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.
The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than the ones of Culhane’s character. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed season two of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

articles.title_zh: 'Open your eyes': Why China's sixth Antarctic base is raising concerns - ABC News & Headlines
articles.content_orig:
China's research icebreaker Xuelong is part of its growing expansion in Antarctica. ( Huang Taoming/Xinhua via AFP )
China is preparing to build its sixth research station in Antarctica, expanding into Marie Byrd Land — a remote, little-studied stretch of the continent's west.
It has some experts and politicians worried.
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie is among those concerned about Australia's defence priorities.
"Five bases have already been built, and China claims there is no geopolitical motive," she said.
Whether that alarm is warranted depends on who you ask.
A new radio telescope installed by China's Antarctica team. ( Xinhua via AFP )
China says the new base, which it plans to build next year, will support research into climate change, ice sheets and marine systems.
And it is far from the only country with a significant presence.
The US operates three permanent year-round bases. So does Australia, which claims 42 per cent of the continent, while Russia has five year-round stations.
But experts warn what matters most is not the station itself.
It is what the project might signal about China's deepening influence inside the institutions that govern Antarctica.
China's proposed new station is in Marie Byrd Land. ( ABC News: Cordelia Brown )
Jiliang Chen, a lecturer in Antarctic law and governance at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania, sees the new station mainly as a matter of prestige.
"Building a station is China capitalising on its strength in this strategic game," Mr Chen said.
China's new station is being developed as per the Antarctic Treaty System's environmental assessment procedures.
Under the Antarctic Treaty, member states cannot veto a proposed new station.
The treaty was originally signed by 12 countries in 1959 and designed to ensure the use of the area for peaceful purposes only and the protection of the environment.
China's scientific expedition team constructing Qinling Station two years ago. ( Zhou Yuan/Xinhua via AFP )
Mr Chen said a stronger physical presence helped consolidate China's role in future decisions on the continent.
"It gives people one more thing to be proud of, scientists more facilities to do research, and more projects to plan," he said.
One complication is that equipment such as satellite systems, communications hardware, aircraft and drones serve civilian research and can easily be adapted for military use.
That dual-use capability is why Mr Chen believes inspection and transparency matter most.
Other experts are more suspicious.
Elizabeth Buchanan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), points to China's existing satellite ground stations and its Military-Civil Fusion policy, which enables civilian companies to develop or supply technologies for military use.
Her deeper worry is that China's spread of stations could eventually let it operate across Antarctica without depending on other countries.
West Antarctica has not been heavily researched. ( Supplied: Matt Burke )
Some say that framing is overblown.
The Antarctic Treaty prohibits military bases, weapons and new territorial claims, while permitting military personnel and equipment for peaceful purposes.
China's embassy in Canberra told the ABC it was "fully committed to ensuring its activities in the region strictly align with the Antarctic Treaty System".
Tony Press, the former head of the Australian Antarctic Division, said he believed mining and military fears were exaggerated, citing the cost and difficulty of moving people and equipment across such a hostile environment.
Unlike China's year-round Quinling station , the new base would run only in summer, hardly the profile of a strategic outpost, Mr Press said.
Instead, he said China was making a geopolitical statement.
"China is obviously doing the old strategic thing of making sure they've got stations around Antarctica that demonstrate quite clearly that they are a big player in, and have an interest in, all parts of Antarctica," he said.
China opened its fifth station, Qinling, in 2024. ( YouTube: China News Service )
Analysts say China is finding ways to become increasingly influential without breaking the rules.
China joined the treaty later than other countries, in 1983.
"China has always been nervous about natural resources and probably more hungry for economic growth," Mr Chen said.
Fishing is where this showed most clearly, he said.
China joined the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), largely because of its interest in Antarctic fishing, Mr Chen said.
China has invested in icebreakers alongside building new bases. ( Huang Taoming/Xinhua via AFP )
Ms Buchanan pointed to the broader growth of China's fishing fleet and domestically built fleet of icebreakers as part of its "Polar Silk Road" strategy.
She said China was also preparing to unveil a nuclear-powered icebreaker, which she said would reduce its reliance on gateway ports such as Hobart.
China is limiting the size of its high sea fishing fleet, except for the polar regions, Mr Chen said.
Antarctic krill fishing is an exception in China's plan for high sea fishing.
Many of Antarctica's emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure. ( Supplied: Klein & Hubert/WWF )
China has generally opposed new marine protected areas in Antarctica.
Nearly half of Antarctica's 60 emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure since 2016 as sea ice they depend on has retreated, according to researchers from the British Antarctic Survey.
Efforts to list them as a Special Protected Species have stalled at CCAMLR, blocked by China and Russia.
The stated objections cite insufficient scientific evidence, or argue that such a listing would address a symptom (habitat loss) rather than its underlying cause of climate change, which sits outside the treaty's scope.
Lyn Goldsworthy, an adjunct researcher at the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies, said China was operating from a strategic perspective, and wanted to avoid restricting access to certain areas in case it had "certain aspirations" in the future.
Ms Goldsworthy added China appeared to join the conservation body CCAMLR for the purpose of fishing first, not marine biology or conservation.
Krill is another source of tension.
The tiny crustaceans are a primary food source for penguins and whales.
Next month's CCAMLR meeting, known as the "Krill Convention", will debate fishing limits.
China has a particular interest in Antarctic krill, which is increasingly valuable as an ingredient in aquaculture feed and nutritional supplements.
Emperor penguins have suffered after record-low Antarctic sea ice. ( Supplied: Bryan and Cherry Alexander/WWF )
Krill products were pulled from shelves in Australian supermarkets after environmental campaigns, but China and Norway are pushing to raise the current catch limit much higher.
Ms Goldsworthy described years of stalemate.
"You have China saying, 'We don't believe in marine protected areas, you should give us our krill fishery'. Other countries are saying, 'No, we won't discuss krill fishery expansion until we've progressed marine protected areas,'" she said.
"There is now a deep distrust."
The underlying ecological concern that over-concentration of fishing in certain areas damages predator populations and habitats has become inseparable from the geopolitics around it, Ms Goldsworthy said.
One flashpoint was an area where heavy Chinese fishing activity overlapped with an Argentine-Chilean proposal for a marine protected area, she said.
Experts say Russia has also played a "disruptive" role, objecting alongside China to new marine protection sites.
China has been increasing its number of bases for scientific research. ( Xinhua via AFP )

articles.title_orig: Rui Pinto, the whistleblower whose leaks prompted investigations into Man City
articles.title_zh: Rui Pinto, the whistleblower whose leaks prompted investigations into Man City
articles.content_orig:
Mention Rui Pinto's name to Manchester City fans outside Etihad Stadium, and you mostly get blank faces.
But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work.
Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City.
Through his website Football Leaks, he published a cache of confidential club documents, including internal emails about sponsorship deals and payments.
That ultimately led to the Premier League charges for breaching of financial rules and Friday's news that the club had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 counts.
For some, 37-year-old Pinto is no more than a criminal who stole information with sinister intentions.
To others, though, he is a bastion of truth who has shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.
BBC Sport has been on a journey across Europe to find out more about the mysterious figure who was the catalyst for so much controversy.
We spoke to one of Pinto's former teachers, a Portuguese politician fighting for him to be protected as a whistleblower, journalists who published the leaks, and a former financial adviser at Manchester City .
And we sat just a few feet from Pinto in the latest of his court cases.
With his cherubic face and spiky hair, Pinto is instantly recognisable. And it seems he hasn't changed.
It is how Mario Falcao, his former geography teacher, remembers him.
In a small courtyard garden in Portugal, we got a glimpse of what Pinto was like as a boy.
"Rui was a perfectly normal pupil. He was nice, with his spiky hair, he was quite sociable but not extrovert," Falcao said.
"He had a good relationship with the teachers, although he did miss these classes quite often. His father was always on top of things, so in the end he passed quite easily."
Did he spot a strong interest in computers in a young Pinto?
"Certainly he was very good in computers. All the work that he did for various courses were very good, when he put his mind to it," his former teacher explained.
The now-retired Falcao speaks fondly of Pinto, who he says behaved just like his friends and would "go to the gym, go to McDonald's".
Pinto had a modest upbringing. He grew up in an area called Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the Douro River from Porto, Portugal's second-largest city. We visited the road where he used to live, which featured tile-fronted houses with terracotta roofs.
His school, Escola Secundaria Almeida Garrett, was well-regarded and was known by locals as 'the university'.
His father, Francisco, worked in a shoe factory and later as an antiques dealer. His mother had died when he was 11.
Falcao said he never predicted what was to come of his former pupil.
"We were very surprised," he said of the moment Pinto was named as the founder of Football Leaks in 2019.
"We weren't imagining anything like this could happen, that he could have problems with justice.
"I certainly wouldn't wish him and his family to be in this situation. Perhaps it was a question of the excesses of youth, his ability with computers, and maybe an excess of club-ism."
"So, you know, the fact that he supported FC Porto prompted him to commit some acts, but maybe he also felt the need for justice that young people very often do feel."

Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City
We visited the street where Rui Pinto grew up in Portugal
Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football".
Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John".
"It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important."
Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums.
"We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela.
"You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion."
It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted.
The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto.
Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar.
Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him.
It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen.
Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team.
"In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said.
"If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work.
"It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context and you can see if there's any reliability issues.
"We always need to make sure that it's authentic material and whenever we publish something about it, it needs to be in the public interest to start writing."
Winterbach finally met Pinto in person in 2019, when he was being held in prison in Lisbon awaiting his trial. He conducted another interview with Pinto in witness protection, in a secret location with high security, describing the arrangements for getting there as being "like a Hollywood movie".
He said: "Rui Pinto is not very tall. He has very distinctive hair, like spiky hair. He usually has red cheeks and he's a youthful, cheeky, funny character. He's friendly and warm when you meet him.
"He's a very impressive character, he's very focused, he's very concentrated. He's very, very intelligent. He's very idealistic about the topics that he uncovered.
"He's one of the most important whistleblowers that we have in Europe or maybe the world."
In all, Pinto provided more than three terabytes - equivalent to about 3,000 copies of the Encyclopedia Britannica - of information to Der Spiegel and other outlets in the European Investigative Collaborations consortium.
We encountered stark contrasts in perceptions of Pinto wherever we went.
Former Portuguese politician and diplomat Ana Gomes has also met Pinto in prison and testified on his behalf at one of his trials. She is firmly of the view that he deserves to be protected, not prosecuted.
"What he has exposed is very important. In Portugal, definitely he is by far the most important whistleblower," the former Member of the European Parliament told us in Lisbon.
"He should be made an ally of our judicial and criminal investigative authorities. He has helped the authorities of other European countries in going after the corrupt and the criminals, instead of being the subject of this judicial prosecution by the choice of our public prosecutors."
When asked what she would say to Manchester City , who had their emails hacked by him, her answer is blunt.
"I couldn't care less. If they have nothing to hide, what's their problem?"

articles.content_orig:
Week 4 boasted the best slate of games on paper of the 2026 season to date, and the action on the field lived up to the hype with the cream rising to the top in ranked showdowns across the country.
The story of the day was No. 20 Oregon going on the road and taking down No. 12 USC, 41-27. The Ducks were road favorites against their long-time rivals, but after star quarterback Dante Moore left the game on a stretcher after a violent late hit on a slide, no one was quite sure what Oregon would look like with backup Dylan Raiola.
The answer was "incredible," as Raiola threw for 289 yards and two touchdowns in a phenomenal performance stepping in suddenly for the injured Moore to lead the Ducks to a much-needed victory. Moore was taken to a local hospital and had feeling in his extremities after the scary hit to his head, but his status going forward remains in question as he undergoes further testing and evaluation.
The Big Ten had a pair of surprising upsets earlier in the day, with No. 17 Iowa taking down No. 18 Michigan 20-19 in The Big House on a last-second touchdown pass. Then No. 13 Penn State got stunned at home by Wisconsin in a 24-20 loss after the Badgers hit a 70-yard touchdown in the closing minutes to pull off a massive upset.
In the SEC, No. 1 Texas survived a road test agaainst No. 14 Tennessee in a 20-17 win that included a wild finish where the Volunteers had a chance to tie or win after getting an onside kick but could not get into range. No. 21 Florida then blew out No. 4 Ole Miss, 52-28, running all over the Rebels in another dominant offensive performance to remain undefeated and hand Ole Miss its first loss.
In the evening, No. 10 LSU dominated No. 23 Texas A&M in a 35-6 rout, setting off alarm bells in College Station after a second straight lopsided loss. The other ranked battle in the SEC featured two surprise teams, as No. 24 Mississippi State outlasted No. 19 Missouri, 31-24, behind another phenomenal performance from this year's breakout star at quarterback, Kamario Taylor.

Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor capped a five-play, 85-yard drive with a 24-yard touchdown pass with 3:57 to play to give the Bulldogs their first top-25 win for his program since 2014. Taylor finished with 360 yards passing and three touchdowns, his fourth straight start with three or more touchdown passes — a first in program history.
Taylor led consecutive touchdown drives in the fourth quarter after his team had fallen behind 24-17 in the second half. Mississippi State is 4-0 in consecutive seasons for the first time since 1944-45.
The Bulldogs had just one SEC win over Jeff Lebby's first two seasons as coach and are now 2-0 in the conference this season.
"We're trying to take the next step and we've got so much out in front of us," Lebby said.
When Oregon saw star quarterback Dante Moore leave the game on a stretcher in the second quarter trailing 10-7, there were serious concerns for the Ducks in both the short- and long-term. Then backup Dylan Raiola stepped in and kept the Ducks' offense rolling, leading five touchdown drives for the Ducks in a dominant performance in the Coliseum, as they eventually pulled away from the Trojans for a 14-point win.
Raiola finished the game 19-of-25 for 289 yards and two touchdowns in a wildly impressive showing after being thrust into action suddenly. The win keeps Oregon's hopes of competing for a Big Ten title and a College Football Playoff berth alive, and Raiola's individual performance provides optimism that he can keep the Ducks at that elite level for however long Moore's absence lasts. Moore had feeling in his extremities after taking a vicious late hit on a slide, but was taken to a hospital for evaluations and we won't know more on his condition until they're don with testing and examinations.
On the other side, it's the continuation of a frustrating trend at USC, where they've been outclassed by top competition in the Lincoln Riley era. The defense had no answers for the Ducks and while Jayden Maiava kept the Trojans in it as long as he could, the offense wasn't quite sharp enough to keep pace in a shootout. Now Riley will face tough questions in what felt like a make or break year as the Trojans get set to hit the meat of their Big Ten schedule with some tough opponents on the horizon including Ohio State and Indiana.
It's been a back-and-forth affair all night in Starkville, but Kamario Taylor has put the home team on top with an incredible sequence of throws in the first quarter. After a deep ball down the left sideline to a fully laid out Anthony Evans III, Taylor threw a dart over the middle to Sanfrisco Magee to put the Bulldogs on top with under four to play.
Now it's on Austin Simmons to find the answer for Mizzou in what's been one of the most entertaining games of the night.
The shootout in the Coliseum continues with another touchdown pass from Dylan Raiola. The Oregon backup has come in and stepped up in a big way, with his latest touchdown on a moon ball to Dakorien Moore, who shook free of the corner and then was able to rise up for a contested catch as the ball hung in the air for seemingly forever before getting to him.
Perhaps more impressive than the Ducks scoring again on USC's porous defense is that they were able to get a stop on the ensuing USC drive, stopping a 4th and 7 attempt by USC at midfield to take over with a chance to go up two scores.
The last time Oklahoma State won a Big 12 conference game was Nov. 25, 2023, when Alan Bowman was quarterback and Ollie Gordon was a first-year starter. Nearly three years later, the 18-game conference losing streak is over after the Cowboys overcame an early deficit to beat West Virginia 41-24.
Cowboys wide receiver Wyatt Young took over the game in the second half, finishing with eight catches for 192 yards and a touchdown out of the slot. articles.title_orig: Grading Florida football after Ole Miss game: What earned an A, what needs work
articles.title_zh: Grading Florida football after Ole Miss game: What earned an A, what needs work
articles.content_orig:
Last December, Florida athletic director Scott Stricklin did more than just kick the proverbial Lane Kiffin tires.
But when it was clear that he'd be headed to Baton Rouge, Stricklin turned to, at that point, a little-known former Kentucky linebacker who'd led Troy and Tulane to successful seasons. Nine months later, Jon Sumrall's Gators are the toast of college football after a drubbing of the Ole Miss Rebels on Saturday . Florida's ability to control the line of scrimmage and move the ball on the ground may present serious problems for the rest of the league.
Despite a 24-point win over a top-five team Saturday, Sumrall quipped to reporters afterward, "We have not arrived."
No, Jon, you have. Florida vaults into our Top 10 at No. 3.
Plenty other wildness transpired on the fourth full Saturday of college football. In the Big Ten, for instance, Iowa (over Michigan) and Wisconsin (over Penn State) picked up comeback wins on the road, and Oregon gashed through USC's defense even without starting quarterback Dante Moore . In the SEC, the Longhorns remain our top-ranked squad after beating Tennessee, Alabama QB Keelon Russell seems like the real deal and OU's Brent Venables owes the Sooners back that contract extension. If you're wondering why more than half of our Top 10 is from the SEC, look at the non-conference power league records (the SEC was the only power conference with a winning record — 10-2 — against the others over the first three weeks).
Florida quarterback Aaron Philo had plenty reason to celebrate after the Gators' blowout win over Ole Miss on Saturday. (Matt Pendleton-Imagn Images)
In the Big 12, Utah cracked our Top 10. In fact, are the Utes the best of the Big 12? They've certainly played the toughest schedule yet of the challengers in the conference. With a win at Louisville, Wake Forest made it more difficult to answer a vexing question: Who the heck will challenge Miami in the ACC?
Let's hit the rankings, which, no, don't yet include Indiana (wins over North Texas, Howard, Western Kentucky and Northwestern don't get you ranked).
This week: beat Tennessee 20-17
No program in the country has the combination of two wins like Texas: Ohio State and at Tennessee. The Longhorns tried to cough it up late in Neyland Stadium, but they hung on to give QB Arch Manning a win at a special place (he wears jersey No. 16 because of uncle Peyton 's years in Knoxville). In an odd stat, Arch was sacked more times (6) than he threw incompletions (five). His 18-yard, third-down strike to Ryan Wingo on Texas' eight-play, 60-yard touchdown drive helped Steve Sarkisian's guys take a 10-point lead.
This week: beat Illinois 42-19
Last week, the Heisman Trophy seemed destined to head to Oxford and into the hands of QB Trinidad Chambliss. This week, it feels like it's right back to where it was originally: in Columbus in the glue-coated hands of Jeremiah Smith. The Buckeyes receiver and future NFL top-10 pick continued a heater of a season with 217 yards, 12 catches and four touchdowns on Saturday. He's up to more than 600 yards through four games and seven scores. He's a magician with his hands, catching nearly everything within a 2-mile radius.
This week: beat Ole Miss 52-28
Shocked? Don't be. The Gators have two wins in very impressive ways, scoring 44 points in a win at Auburn and then 52 against Ole Miss in The Swamp. First-year coach Jon Sumrall's team plays a physical brand of football that's fun to watch. They've rushed for nearly 550 yards in consecutive SEC games. That's no easy task. QB Aaron Philo is playing smart, consistent football and the Gators look like legit contenders in the league.
This week: beat Central Michigan 52-3
QB Darian Mensah's numbers through his first four games are simply absurd. Get this: He's got 12 incompletions — twelve! — and 14 touchdowns. Don't ignore that he's thrown for at least 330 yards twice, too. His favorite target, Malachi Toney (Baby Jesus!) caught another six passes for 120 yards on Saturday. The Hurricanes are as explosive as they've been the last few years. Can they continue the onslaught against a Clemson team that's, sort of, found some momentum?
Alabama QB Keelon Russell put on a show Saturday with four passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown in a blowout win over South Carolina. (David Leong-Imagn Images)
This week: beat South Carolina 49-18
Next week: at Mississippi State
Perhaps it's time to start talking about QB Keelon Russell in relation to the Heisman Trophy, no? He's completing more than 70 percent of his passes, has eight touchdowns and two picks. On Saturday against the Gamecocks, Russell misfired on just six passes and threw four touchdowns. He's got plenty of pieces around him too. Kane Wommack's defense held South Carolina to a 21 percent clip on third downs.
This week: lost to Florida 52-28
The Rebels need the bye next week. After an emotional victory against former coach Lane Kiffin and LSU, they laid the egg in Gainesville without star running back Kewan Lacy. The Gators' defense swallowed Ole Miss' ground attack and pressured Trinidad Chambliss just enough. But the most concerning thing for Pete Golding is his defense, which was exploited earlier this year against Louisville, nearly collapsed in the second half against LSU and allowed almost 500 yards on Saturday.
This week: beat Purdue 49-10
Next week: at North Carolina
The Irish's schedule isn't glamorous so far. In fact, they haven't beaten a team that will finish ranked inside the top 25 at the end of the season (at least that's our assumption about Wisconsin, Rice, Michigan State and Purdue). But the wins are fairly dominant and despite the struggles at times to run the football, Marcus Freeman's defense is one salty group. They entered third in the country in total D — a ranking that won't move much after Purdue's 218 yards.
This week: beat Oklahoma 41-13
The Bulldogs haven't played the toughest schedule so far, which is why they're at No. 8. But between QB Gunner Stockton and Kirby Smart's defense, they appear to be legitimate SEC title contenders — again. On Saturday, they forced the Sooners into a plethora of mistakes, including two fumbles, an interception and a turnover on downs. It's no fun playing against the Dawgs defense, despite NIL and the portal making it more difficult for them to stockpile front-seven depth.
This week: beat Missouri 31-24
Get ready to hear a whole lot about a Mississippi kid named Kamario Taylor, the Bulldogs' electric sophomore starting quarterback. He's slung 14 touchdowns and just two picks and, most recently on Saturday, put up 360 yards passing against Missouri in State's first top-25 win in more than a decade. Are the Bulldogs perfect? No. The defense can be exploited but former head coach Zach Arnett, the defensive coordinator, has the unit playing good enough.
This week: beat Iowa State 31-17
Welcome to the Top 10, Utes! They nearly let a 17-point lead slip away, but QB Devon Dampier showed just how slippery he can be. Most folks thought Dampier might follow Kyle Whittingham to Ann Arbor. Not so fast! He stuck around with new coach Morgan Scalley, who's got Utah playing its always-dependable D. On Saturday, RB Wayshawn Parker had a breakout performance (18 carries for 174 yards and three total TDs).
