articles.title_zh: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Godzilla and King Ghidorah Battle to the Death in the Even Grander Follow-Up to ‘Godzilla Minus One’
articles.content_orig:
The humanistic heroes of the first film return, and so does writer-director Takashi Yamazaki's awesome sense of monster action paintings in motion.
Of all the criticisms leveled at Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” (apart from the one I have: that the entire movie is a frigging mess), the most resonant, to me, was the complaint that Nolan had made a mistake by leaving the Greek gods out of the story. He certainly demonstrated that you could make a version of Homer minus the gods; he didn’t necessarily show that it could be done without losing a crucial dimension. Besides, if you can’t see gods at a movie of “The Odyssey,” where are you going to see them?
The answer is: at a Japanese monster movie — more thrilling, by leagues, than “The Odyssey” — where the monsters possess an ominous majesty that’s not of this world, even as they’re in the middle of laying waste to it.
In “ Godzilla Minus Zero ,” which premiered tonight at the New York Film Festival (it opens Nov. 6), there are two oversize mystic beasts: Godzilla, the original kaiju (the character is now 72 years old, proving that 72 is the new awesome), and King Ghidorah, the dragon hydra who made his first appearance in the 1964 kaiju classic “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster.” Each is a formidable creature, though in both cases it’s more than a matter of epic stomp or gargantuan wing power. When Godzilla tilts his head up to the sky, gathers his might, and then shoots out a blast of radioactivity that can level a city, it’s an exhibition of transcendent force . And Ghidorah’s heads — which look, up close, like costume figures out of a Golden Dragon Dance — emit orange lightning volts that extend for half a mile. These aren’t mere monsters. They’re serious movie gods.
“Godzilla Minus Zero” is set in 1949, and it opens with a startling sequence in which Ghidorah, with only one head (this will change), shows up in the city of Matsumoto and destroys it. We’re given a grand vista of demolition, and also close-ups of Ghidorah seen from the point-of-view of Professor Murakami (Min Tanaka), a Hiroshima survivor who’s been doing biological creature research. Godzilla will soon turn up as well, even though he was thought to have been destroyed at the end of “Godzilla Minus One.” (It’s hard to destroy a god.) To save Japan, Kenji Noda (Hidetake Yoshioka), the high-strung, pencil-necked, Einstein-haired director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, leads his team in devising a plan that’s got a sandbox-showdown ingenuity: They will lure both creatures to a single locale and goad them into fighting each other. Whichever one remains standing will be wounded and weakened, and the human forces can then finish that monster off.
When you go to see a big visual-effects movie, like something from Marvel, the closing credits that roll on for 12 minutes will feature multiple armies of visual-effects teams (each digital company with its own general). I have no doubt that a formidable army worked on “Godzilla Minus Zero.” But it’s also a movie that features the highly unusual credit “VFX, written, and directed by Takashi Yamazaki .” That’s a sign of how much the movie’s visual effects emanate directly from the imagination of the filmmaker. He’s writing, he’s directing, and he’s orchestrating spectacular gargantuan action paintings of beasts in motion. He’s an artist of larger-than-life pop horror.
We’ve seen countless monster duels in kaiju movies (old and new, good and bad, Japanese and American), but Yamazaki, who rebooted the genre and took it to a new peak in the revelatory 2023 retro kaiju classic “Godzilla Minus One,” works with a quality that none of the filmmakers of recent decades has summoned: a fairy-tale innocence, an immersion in the annihilating heavy-metal poetry of Godzilla — the way the destruction of a city can become a spectacle out of a dream (which is to say, a national nightmare). In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” when Godzilla and King Ghidorah go at it, it’s more than a WWE match of primeval rivals. It’s a clash of the titans that will reduce everyone in the audience to a wide-eyed, jaw-dropped child.
“Godzilla Minus One” was justly celebrated for its human story, which felt like something out of a Kurosawa movie of the ’50s. In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” Yamazaki follows through on that, continuing the tale of Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), the former World War II kamikaze pilot; Noriko (Minamo Hamabe), who is now his wife; and Akiko (Sae Nagatani), their adopted daughter, who has grown into a verbally precocious seven-year-old. The fate of this family is at the heart of the film’s emotional palette. To battle the creatures, Kōichi will go back into fighter-pilot mode, but the services of Noriko will be called on as well. She’s one of the survivors of Godzilla’s 1947 attack who now has bits of Godzilla DNA embedded in her body (which is why she wears an eyepatch).
For a long time, kaiju movies were a semi-joke — a fusion of the colossal and the cheesy, and the fact that you couldn’t separate the two was part of what gave the genre its unique shlock magic. But Yamazaki transcends all that. His staging draws on our collective nostalgic memory of kaiju grandeur, and it also dignifies the genre by building it on a drama that’s staged with passion and vigor. When did anyone ever talk about performances in a Godzilla movie? But in “Godzilla Minus Zero,” one responds to the high anxiety of Yoshioka’s Noda, and to the magnetic intelligence of Masami Nagasawa as Makoto Aoyama, a meteorologist whose intuition about storms has a hint of the prophetic. Min Tanaka, who plays the professor, is an actor who was born on March 10, 1945, the day of the firebombing of Tokyo (the deadliest air raid in human history), and his courtly but simmering presence powerfully channels the film’s awareness of history. Yamazaki stages a couple of audacious sequences that feel, in their way, like his answer to “Oppenheimer.” One is a fantasy of Godzilla approaching Manhattan the way he once approached Tokyo, a chilling vision for any American to behold.
At first, when the Japanese officials think that they’re contending only with Ghidorah, the film’s battles have a tactical stateliness. Ghidorah heads off to the mountains and hibernates, curling up like a giant snake, which makes them think they can bomb him into oblivion, using planes and weapons borrowed from the U.S. But all that accomplishes is to wake the sleeping giant. The sequence in which a half dozen planes battle Ghidorah in the air is grand, eye-popping filmmaking. And that’s just the appetizer, as Godzilla’s return heralds a battle of staggering vastness.
In the final section, a plot strand or two gets a bit tangled. The professor has a hidden agenda, and how he ever meant to carry it out remains too abstract to be entirely clear. Yet as key characters are put under fire, we realize how much we’ve come to care about these creature battlers. They’re rooted in a time and place that feels all too real, and this allows the monsters to parade their primitive might in a way that means something. It was a stroke of inspiration on Yamazaki’s part to reset the kaiju genre in the late ’40s, during the Atomic Age where it is spiritually rooted (the original “Gojira” was released in 1954). The creators of the new James Bond series would do well to follow suit. (That’s how Bond could be vital again.) “Godzilla Minus Zero” is destined to connect with a huge international audience, and it’s already clear that this won’t be the last of Yamazaki’s kaiju epics. That’s because the movie proves that when you do it right, what seemed old can become timeless.

articles.title_zh: US got pandas from China. Trump needs a lot more than that | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title_orig: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.title_zh: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

articles.title_orig: Florida surges into CFP conversation after trouncing Ole Miss as Jon Sumrall eyes SEC coaching history
articles.title_zh: Florida surges into CFP conversation after trouncing Ole Miss as Jon Sumrall eyes SEC coaching history
articles.content_orig:
We'll be seeing ample Gator chomps the rest of the way this season.
Coming out of Saturday's 52-28 statement win over previously unbeaten and No. 4 Ole Miss , the No. 21 Gators look the part in the early season College Football Playoff conversation and have a surging Heisman candidate leading their backfield in Jadan Baugh .
Jon Sumrall is trying to become the fifth first-year coach all-time to reach the CFP in his first campaign. He'd join four others across the Power Four to accomplish that feat, but would make history as the first from the SEC.
The win for the Gators snapped a four-game losing skid against ranked competition and was Florida's first victory over a top-five opponent since 2020 ( Georgia ).
The Gators had lost their previous 12 matchups against the nation's elite, and Sumrall joked that, coming into Saturday's showdown, his team has no business being favored against the Rebels .
The telling sign of a well-coached team with no signs of wilting is its ability to respond, and the Gators reflected that in the third quarter, absorbing body blows before punching back.
Florida broke open a 24-21 game in the second half with consecutive touchdown drives predicated by the power running of Baugh and Duke Clark along with quarterback Aaron Philo's precision on third down.
Ole Miss entered Week 4 with the SEC's worst rush defense, giving up 159 yards per game, and nothing changed inside Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. Baugh and Clark combined for 268 yards on the ground, both eclipsing the 100-yard barrier — the first time that's happened in the same game for Florida since 2022.
That's part of the new identity Sumrall mentioned earlier this week.
"I think our mindset has changed," Sumrall said. "I think we're playing with a different level of resiliency and toughness than what I felt like was going on here when I got here. And I think our guys expect to win. So that's one component I think that I'm pleased with. How we play the game, some detail, some consistency.
"There's a lot of areas where you still have to improve upon a lot to become the type of team we want to be long term. And so we're a long way from a finished product here. We haven't even begun to scratch the surface for what my vision is for how we play this game week in, week out."
That's two SEC tests and two wins for a first-year coach who has Florida looking like a factor — not only in the SEC race — in the national championship discussion. Sumrall inherited a talented roster, but he deserves credit for getting this much out of it this quickly.
For the first time since 2021, Florida will be a top-15 team in Sunday's new AP poll entering October with all of the program's lofty goals still out front. It's a weekly grind in the SEC, and anything can happen over the Gators' final eight games, but this looks like a team capable of reaching the CFP and being a tough out, given this roster embodies its coach's mindset.
Sumrall said his players looked "a little bit over-amped" after the first quarter ended with a failed fourth-and-2 conversion try at the Rebels' 19-yard line. Florida had a comfortable 10-point lead, and Philo had a man open in the flat for a potential touchdown but failed to execute.
In the past, the Gators' offense might have folded after that or struggled to regain confidence with Trinidad Chambliss and an elite passing game on the other sideline. However, all of the opposition's counter jabs were answered with force as Florida barged its way into the national spotlight.
With Buster Faulkner calling the plays and a renewed focus on physicality off the snap, the Gators are scoring points in bunches with an onslaught of explosive plays. Florida's 214 points are the most through the first four games of a season since 1996 — when the Gators won the national title under Steve Spurrier.
Elite territory for Sumrall and Co.
